arXiv:2508.12467v1 [math.CO] 17 Aug 2025

Log-concavity of rows of triangular arrays satisfying a certain super-recurrence

Umesh Shankar ††thanks: 204093001@iitb.ac.in, umeshshankar@outlook.com Affiliation: Department of Mathematics, Indian Institute of Technology Bombay, Mumbai 400076, India
August 24, 2026
Abstract

Recurrences of the form

T⁡(n,k)=(α​n+β​k+γ)​T​(n−1,k)+(α′​n+β′​k+γ′)​T​(n−1,k−1)+δn,0​δk,0.T(n,k)=(\alpha n+\beta k+\gamma)\ T(n-1,k)+(\alpha^{\prime}n+\beta^{\prime}k+\gamma^{\prime})\ T(n-1,k-1)+\delta_{n,0}\delta_{k,0}.

show up as the recurrence for many well-studied combinatorial sequences such as the Stirling numbers of first and second kind, the Lah numbers, Eulerian numbers etc. Recently, many of these sequences have received generalisations that obey a recurrence of the form

T⁡(n,k)=(α​n+β​k+γ)l​T​(n−1,k)+(α′​n+β′​k+γ′)l​T​(n−1,k−1)+δn,0​δk,0.T(n,k)=(\alpha n+\beta k+\gamma)^{l}\ T(n-1,k)+(\alpha^{\prime}n+\beta^{\prime}k+\gamma^{\prime})^{l}\ T(n-1,k-1)+\delta_{n,0}\delta_{k,0}.

where ll is a positive integer. Many of these generalised sequences also satisfy properties such as unimodality, log-concavity, gamma-nonnegativity, real-rootedness that the original sequences satisfy. In this article, we give sufficient conditions for rows of triangular arrays, arising from the recurrence stated above, to be log-concave. We show that our sufficient condition is satisfied by many of the classical examples, thereby giving a new unified approach to proving their log-concavity. This sufficient condition also confirms a conjecture of Tankosič [20] about the log-concavity of generalised Lah numbers.

Our main technique will be to interpret the triangular array (T⁡(n,k))(T(n,k)) as weighted lattice paths and produce an injection that is increasing in weight. Finally, we introduce a two-parameter generalisation of the Eulerian numbers analogous to the generalised Stirling and Lah counterparts. We prove that this sequence is palindromic and make some remarks about their gamma-nonnegativity and real-rootedness.

1 Introduction

Let ℕ\mathbb{N} denote the set of non-negative integers and for n∈ℕn\in\mathbb{N}, let [n][n] denote the set {1,2,…,n}\{1,2,\dotsc,n\}. A finite sequence of real numbers (ak)k=0n(a_{k})_{k=0}^{n} is said to be log-concave if ak2≥ak+1​ak−1a_{k}^{2}\geq a_{k+1}a_{k-1} for all indices k∈[n−1]k\in[n-1]. Log-concavity is a well-studied property of finite sequences and it appears in various areas of mathematics such as combinatorics, probability and algebra. See the surveys of Stanley [18], Branden [5] for a wealth of results on log-concavity.

A triangular array T⁡(n,k)T(n,k) is a collection of real numbers that satisfies a recurrence of the form

T⁡(n,k)=c⁡(n,k)​T​(n−1,k)+d⁡(n,k)​T​(n−1,k−1)+δn,0​δk,0,for ​n,k≥0,T(n,k)=c(n,k)\ T(n-1,k)+d(n,k)\ T(n-1,k-1)+\delta_{n,0}\delta_{k,0},\qquad\text{for }n,k\geq 0, (1.1)

and T⁡(n,k)=0T(n,k)=0 for n<0n<0, k<0k<0, or k>nk>n, for some c⁡(n,k),d⁡(n,k)∈ℝc(n,k),d(n,k)\in\mathbb{R} and δi,j\delta_{i,j} is the Kronecker delta function. Several interesting enumerative sequences obey a recurrence of this form, including the binomial numbers, (nk)\binom{n}{k}, the Stirling numbers of the first and second kinds, s⁡(n,k)s(n,k) and S⁡(n,k)S(n,k), the Lah numbers, L⁡(n,k)L(n,k), and the Eulerian numbers, A⁡(n,k)A(n,k). These sequences and their generating functions are rich in combinatorial structure, and well-studied in the literature, in particular with respect to properties such as log-concavity, unimodality, gamma positivity, and real-rootedness. Moreover, in all these examples we have that the expressions for c⁡(n,k)c(n,k) and d⁡(n,k)d(n,k) are affine functions in the variables nn and kk.

To prove the log-concavity of the Stirling numbers of both kinds, Kurtz [8] gave the following sufficient condition for triangular arrays.

Theorem 1.1 ([8, Theorem 2]).

Let T⁡(n,k)=c⁡(n,k)​T​(n−1,k)+d⁡(n,k)​T​(n−1,k−1)T(n,k)=c(n,k)\ T(n-1,k)+d(n,k)\ T(n-1,k-1) and

  • •

    2​c​(n,k)≥c⁡(n,k−1)+c⁡(n,k+1),2c(n,k)\geq c(n,k-1)+c(n,k+1),

  • •

    2​d​(n,k)≥d⁡(n,k−1)+d⁡(n,k+1),2d(n,k)\geq d(n,k-1)+d(n,k+1),

then, the array T⁡(n,k)T(n,k) is log-concave in kk, for all nn.

A strengthening of the Theorem was obtained by Sagan [15] wherein the hypothesis of concavity of the coefficients was weakened to log-concavity of the coefficients and concavity of the product. The theorem is as follows.

Theorem 1.2 ([15, Theorem 1]).

Let T⁡(n,k)T(n,k) be an extended triangular array satisfying T⁡(n,k)=c⁡(n,k)​T​(n−1,k)+d⁡(n,k)​T​(n−1,k−1)T(n,k)=c(n,k)\ T(n-1,k)+d(n,k)\ T(n-1,k-1) for all n≥1n\geq 1 and T⁡(n,k),c⁡(n,k),d⁡(n,k)T(n,k),c(n,k),d(n,k) are all non-negative integers. Suppose

  • •

    c⁡(n,k),d⁡(n,k)c(n,k),d(n,k) are log-concave in kk,

  • •

    d⁡(n,k−1)​c​(n,k+1)+d⁡(n,k+1)​c​(n,k−1)≤2​d​(n,k)​c​(n,k)d(n,k-1)c(n,k+1)+d(n,k+1)c(n,k-1)\leq 2d(n,k)c(n,k),

then, the T⁡(n,k)T(n,k) are log-concave in kk.

Recently, some of the enumerative sequences listed above have been generalized by introducing more parameters. Let r∈ℕr\in\mathbb{N}.The rr-Stirling number of the first kind, sr​(n,k)s_{r}(n,k) (with n≥k≥rn\geq k\geq r), is defined to be the number of permutations in 𝔖n\mathfrak{S}_{n} with kk cycles such that 1,2,…,r1,2,\dotsc,r are in different cycles. The rr-Stirling number of the second kind, Sr​(n,k)S_{r}(n,k) (with n≥k≥rn\geq k\geq r), is defined to be the number of partitions of [n][n] into kk blocks such that 1,2,…,r1,2,\dots,r are in different blocks. These numbers have been studied in great detail, see [6, 12]. The closely related rr-Lah number, Lr​(n,k)L_{r}(n,k) (with n≥k≥rn\geq k\geq r), is defined to be the number of partitions of [n][n] into kk nonempty ordered subsets such that 1,2,…,r1,2,\dots,r are in different ordered subsets. These were studied in [14, 17, 13]. The rr-Stirling numbers and rr-Lah numbers are also triangular arrays in the sense of (1.1), with coefficients that are affine functions in the variables.

These numbers have been further generalised with an additional parameter as follows (see [3, 20]). Let l∈ℕl\in\mathbb{N}. Define the cycle leader of a permutation π∈𝔖n\pi\in\mathfrak{S}_{n}, denoted cl⁡(π)\cl(\pi), to be the set of minimum elements of each cycle in the cycle decomposition of π\pi. The (l,r)(l,r)-Stirling number of the first kind, sr(l)​(n,k)s_{r}^{(l)}(n,k), is defined to be the number of ll-tuples of permutations (π1,…,πl)(\pi_{1},\dotsc,\pi_{l}) such that [r]⊂cl⁡(π1)[r]\subset\cl(\pi_{1}) and cl⁡(π1)=⋯=cl⁡(πl)\cl(\pi_{1})=\dotsb=\cl(\pi_{l}). Define the block leader of a partition Π\Pi of [n][n], denoted bl⁡(Π)\bl(\Pi), to be the set of minimum elements of each block of the partition Π\Pi. The (l,r)(l,r)-Stirling number of the second kind, Sr(l)​(n,k)S_{r}^{(l)}(n,k), is defined similarly: it is the number of ll-tuples of partitions (Π1,…,Πl)(\Pi_{1},\dotsc,\Pi_{l}) such that [r]⊂bl⁡(Π1)[r]\subset\bl(\Pi_{1}) and bl⁡(Π1)=⋯=bl⁡(Πl)\bl(\Pi_{1})=\dotsb=\bl(\Pi_{l}). The (l,r)(l,r)-Lah number is defined in a similar manner to the (l,r)(l,r)-Stirling number of the second kind. It counts the number of ll-tuples of partitions (Π1,…,Πl)(\Pi_{1},\dotsc,\Pi_{l}) into kk linearly ordered blocks such that [r]⊂bl⁡(Π1)[r]\subset\bl(\Pi_{1}) and bl⁡(Π1)=⋯=bl⁡(Πl)\bl(\Pi_{1})=\dotsb=\bl(\Pi_{l}).

The (l,r)(l,r)-Stirling numbers and (l,r)(l,r)-Lah numbers are also triangular arrays; in particular, equation (1.1) for these numbers take the following forms:

sr(l)​(n,k)\displaystyle s_{r}^{(l)}(n,k) =(n−1)l​sr(l)​(n−1,k)+sr(l)​(n−1,k−1)\displaystyle=(n-1)^{l}s_{r}^{(l)}(n-1,k)+s_{r}^{(l)}(n-1,k-1)
Sr(l)​(n,k)\displaystyle S_{r}^{(l)}(n,k) =kl​Sr(l)​(n−1,k)+Sr(l)​(n−1,k−1)\displaystyle=k^{l}S_{r}^{(l)}(n-1,k)+S_{r}^{(l)}(n-1,k-1)
Lr(l)​(n,k)\displaystyle L_{r}^{(l)}(n,k) =(n+k−1)l​Lr(l)​(n−1,k)+Lr(l)​(n−1,k−1)\displaystyle=(n+k-1)^{l}L_{r}^{(l)}(n-1,k)+L_{r}^{(l)}(n-1,k-1)

for 1≤r≤k≤n1\leq r\leq k\leq n. While it is easy to show that the (l,r)(l,r)-Stirling numbers of both kinds are log-concave, it was conjectured in [20] that the (l,r)(l,r)-Lah numbers are log-concave in kk as well. However, the theorems of Kurtz and Sagan are not applicable to these arrays when l≥2l\geq 2.

Motivated by the form of the recurrences appearing in the conjecture, we develop a general method to establish log-concavity of many so-called “super-recurrence” relations of the form

T⁡(n,k)=(α​n+β​k+γ)l​T​(n−1,k)+(α′​n+β′​k+γ′)l​T​(n−1,k−1)+δn,0​δk,0,for ​n,k≥0,T(n,k)=(\alpha n+\beta k+\gamma)^{l}\ T(n-1,k)+(\alpha^{\prime}n+\beta^{\prime}k+\gamma^{\prime})^{l}\ T(n-1,k-1)+\delta_{n,0}\delta_{k,0},\quad\text{for }n,k\geq 0, (1.2)

and T⁡(n,k)=0T(n,k)=0 for n<0n<0, k<0k<0, or k>nk>n, where α,α′,β,β′,γ,γ′∈ℕ\alpha,\alpha^{\prime},\beta,\beta^{\prime},\gamma,\gamma^{\prime}\in\mathbb{N}, and δi,j\delta_{i,j} is the Kronecker delta function. We also show that The main result of the paper is a sufficient condition for log-concavity of triangular arrays which is the following.

Theorem 1.3.

For n≥1n\geq 1 and 0<k≤n0<k\leq n, let T⁡(n,k)T(n,k) satisfy the following triangular recurrence.

T⁡(n,k)=c⁡(n,k)​T​(n−1,k)+d⁡(n,k)​T​(n−1,k−1)T(n,k)=c(n,k)\ T(n-1,k)+d(n,k)\ T(n-1,k-1)

The sequence (T⁡(n,k))k=0n(T(n,k))_{k=0}^{n} is log-concave if (i),(i​i)(i),(ii) and (i​i​i)(iii) hold.

  1. (i)

    c⁡(n,k),d⁡(n,k)c(n,k),d(n,k) are log-concave in kk.

  2. (ii)

    Suppose

    • •

    • •

      k2−k1=l2−l1+1k_{2}-k_{1}=l_{2}-l_{1}+1,

    Then,

    c⁡(n1,k1)​d​(n1,k2)​d​(n2,l1)​c​(n2,l2)≤c⁡(n1,k1+1)​d​(n1,k2−1)​d​(n2,l1+1)​c​(n2,l2−1)c(n_{1},k_{1})d(n_{1},k_{2})d(n_{2},l_{1})c(n_{2},l_{2})\leq c(n_{1},k_{1}+1)d(n_{1},k_{2}-1)d(n_{2},l_{1}+1)c(n_{2},l_{2}-1)
  3. (iii)

    For all kk, we have d⁡(n1,k+1)​c​(n1,k)≤d⁡(n1,k)​c​(n1,k+1)d(n_{1},k+1)c(n_{1},k)\leq d(n_{1},k)c(n_{1},k+1).

Using the theorem above, we obtain a sufficient condition for log-concavity of rows of arrays satisfying the Equation (1.2).

Theorem 1.4.

Let α,β,γ\alpha,\beta,\gamma and α′,β′,γ′\alpha^{\prime},\beta^{\prime},\gamma^{\prime} be real numbers such that the following hold:

  1. (i)

    α,α′,β≥0\alpha,\alpha^{\prime},\beta\geq 0

Then

T⁡(n,k)=(α​n+β​k+γ)l​T​(n−1,k)+(α′​n+β′​k+γ′)l​T​(n−1,k−1)T(n,k)=(\alpha n+\beta k+\gamma)^{l}\ T(n-1,k)+(\alpha^{\prime}n+\beta^{\prime}k+\gamma^{\prime})^{l}\ T(n-1,k-1) (1.3)

is log-concave in kk for all nn.

The main technique is to interpret the entries of the triangular array (T⁡(n,k))(T(n,k)) in terms of weighted lattice paths, which we describe in the next section. Our method allows us to establish the log-concavity of the generalized Stirling and Lah numbers described above, as well as several other well-studied combinatorial sequences, which we list in the Table 1 below.

Motivated by the definitions of the (l,r)(l,r)-Stirling and (l,r)(l,r)-Lah numbers, we generalise the Eulerian numbers to a two parameter (l,r)(l,r)-Eulerian number. A subexceedant function is a function f:[n]→[n]f:[n]\rightarrow[n] such that 0<f⁡(i)≤i0<f(i)\leq i for all i∈[n]i\in[n]. Dumont (see [11]) showed that the Eulerian number 𝒜⁡(n,k)\mathcal{A}(n,k) counts the number of subexceedant functions such that the cardinality of the image of ff is k+1k+1. Similar to the Stirling and Lah counterparts, we define the block leader of a subexceedant function. The block leader of a subexceedant function ff is the set {i∈[n]:f⁡(i)∉f⁡([n−1])}\{i\in[n]:f(i)\notin f([n-1])\}. Let us denote it by bl⁡(f)\bl(f). Note that the |bl⁡(f)||\bl(f)| is the size of the image of ff because for each element in the image of ff the smallest element in the pre-image is in bl⁡(f)\bl(f).

Let ll be a positive integer. Define 𝒜r(l)​(n,k)\mathcal{A}_{r}^{(l)}(n,k) to count the number of ll-tuples (f1,…,fl)(f_{1},\dots,f_{l}) such that [r]⊂bl⁡(f1)[r]\subset\bl(f_{1}), |bl⁡(f1)|=k+1|\bl(f_{1})|=k+1, and bl⁡(f1)=⋯=bl⁡(fl)\bl(f_{1})=\dots=\bl(f_{l}). We show that there is a natural connection between the rr-Stirling numbers and rr-Eulerian numbers (setting l=1l=1), which is done by showing that the rr-Eulerian numbers count the number of permutations in 𝔖n\mathfrak{S}_{n} with kk descents such that [r][r] is subset of the set of first letters of the increasing runs in π\pi. Finally, we show that the associated polynomials of the (l,1)(l,1)-Eulerian numbers are palindromic and make a remark about their gamma-nonnegativity and real-rootedness.

2 Definitions and Preliminaries

Suppose that n≥1n\geq 1 and 0<k≤n0<k\leq n, a triangular recurrence is a recurrence of the form

T⁡(n,k)=c⁡(n,k)​T​(n−1,k)+d⁡(n,k)​T​(n−1,k−1)T(n,k)=c(n,k)\ T(n-1,k)+d(n,k)\ T(n-1,k-1)

with boundary conditions T⁡(1,1)=1T(1,1)=1 and and the coefficients c⁡(n,k),d⁡(n,k)c(n,k),d(n,k) are non-negative real numbers.

For A,B∈ℤ2A,B\in\mathbb{Z}^{2}, we denote by 𝒫A→B\mathcal{P}_{A\rightarrow B} the set of lattice paths starting with AA and ending at BB that use the step N=(0,1)N=(0,1) (north) and the step C=(1,1)C=(1,1) (cross). We can encode these paths as words in the alphabet {N,C}\{N,C\}. For example, we write p=N​C​C​C​N​Np=NCCCNN for the lattice path below.

Since most of the paths in this paper will start from the point (1,1)(1,1), we will write 𝒫A\mathcal{P}_{A} instead of 𝒫(1,1)→A\mathcal{P}_{(1,1)\rightarrow A}.

We shall assign weights to the step of the lattice path. For a north step NN that starts at (k,n−1)(k,n-1) and ends at (k,n)(k,n), we assign the weight c⁡(n,k)c(n,k). For the cross step CC that starts at (k−1,n−1)(k-1,n-1) and ends at (k,n)(k,n), we assign the weight d⁡(n,k)d(n,k).

The weight of a path p∈𝒫A→Bp\in\mathcal{P}_{A\rightarrow B} is the product of the weights of the steps that make up the path. In our running example, it would be c⁡(2,1)​d​(3,2)​d​(4,3)​d​(5,4)​c​(6,4)​c​(7,4)c(2,1)d(3,2)d(4,3)d(5,4)c(6,4)c(7,4).

3 A log-concavity criterion for triangular arrays

3.1 Triangular arrays

We have the following interpretation of a triangular array in terms of weighted lattice paths:

Theorem 3.1.

For n≥1n\geq 1 and 0<k≤n0<k\leq n, let T⁡(n,k)T(n,k) satisfy the following triangular recurrence.

T⁡(n,k)=c⁡(n,k)​T​(n−1,k)+d⁡(n,k)​T​(n−1,k−1).T(n,k)=c(n,k)\ T(n-1,k)+d(n,k)\ T(n-1,k-1).

Then,

T⁡(n,k)=∑p∈𝒫(k,n)wt⁡(p).T(n,k)=\displaystyle\sum_{p\in\mathcal{P}_{(k,n)}}\wt(p).
Proof.

We prove by induction on nn. Each path in 𝒫(k,n)\mathcal{P}_{(k,n)} is either path in 𝒫(k,n−1)\mathcal{P}_{(k,n-1)} followed by an NN step or a path in 𝒫(k−1,n−1)\mathcal{P}_{(k-1,n-1)} followed by a cross step CC. Since the weight of a path is the product of weight of the constituting steps, the statement follows from the recurrence. ∎

Under this interpretation, we have the following interpretation of the log-concavity of rows.

Corollary 3.2.

The rows of the triangular array T⁡(n,k)T(n,k) are log-concave if and only if

∑(p,q)∈𝒫(k+1,n)×𝒫(k−1,n)wt⁡(p)​wt⁡(q)≤∑(p′,q′)∈𝒫(k,n)×𝒫(k,n)wt⁡(p′)​wt⁡(q′)\displaystyle\sum_{(p,q)\in\mathcal{P}_{(k+1,n)}\times\mathcal{P}_{(k-1,n)}}\wt(p)\wt(q)\leq\displaystyle\sum_{(p^{\prime},q^{\prime})\in\mathcal{P}_{(k,n)}\times\mathcal{P}_{(k,n)}}\wt(p^{\prime})\wt(q^{\prime})
Proof.

The inequality T​(n,k)2≥T⁡(n,k−1)​T​(n,k+1)T(n,k)^{2}\geq T(n,k-1)T(n,k+1) is equivalent to

(∑p∈𝒫(k,n)wt⁡(p))2≥(∑p∈𝒫(k−1,n)wt⁡(p))​(∑q∈𝒫(k+1,n)wt⁡(q))\bigg(\displaystyle\sum_{p\in\mathcal{P}_{(k,n)}}\wt(p)\bigg)^{2}\geq\bigg(\displaystyle\sum_{p\in\mathcal{P}_{(k-1,n)}}\wt(p)\bigg)\bigg(\displaystyle\sum_{q\in\mathcal{P}_{(k+1,n)}}\wt(q)\bigg)

This can be written as

∑(p′,q′)∈𝒫(k,n)×𝒫(k,n)wt⁡(p′)​wt⁡(q′)≥∑(p,q)∈𝒫(k+1,n)×𝒫(k−1,n)wt⁡(p)​wt⁡(q).\displaystyle\sum_{(p^{\prime},q^{\prime})\in\mathcal{P}_{(k,n)}\times\mathcal{P}_{(k,n)}}\wt(p^{\prime})\wt(q^{\prime})\geq\displaystyle\sum_{(p,q)\in\mathcal{P}_{(k+1,n)}\times\mathcal{P}_{(k-1,n)}}\wt(p)\wt(q).

This completes our proof. ∎

3.2 An injection from 𝒫(k+1,n)×𝒫(k−1,n)\mathcal{P}_{(k+1,n)}\times\mathcal{P}_{(k-1,n)} to 𝒫(k,n)×𝒫(k,n)\mathcal{P}_{(k,n)}\times\mathcal{P}_{(k,n)}

We shall describe an injective map that sends a pair of paths (p,q)∈𝒫(k+1,n)×𝒫(k−1,n)(p,q)\in\mathcal{P}_{(k+1,n)}\times\mathcal{P}_{(k-1,n)} to a pair of paths (p′,q′)∈𝒫(k,n)×𝒫(k,n)(p^{\prime},q^{\prime})\in\mathcal{P}_{(k,n)}\times\mathcal{P}_{(k,n)}. The injection is based on an idea of Sagan [15] that is used to give injective proofs of log-concavity of the Stirling numbers of first and second kind.

Theorem 3.3 (Discrete Intermediate Value Theorem).

Let ff be an integer-valued function on the integers in the interval [m,n][m,n]. Suppose that |f⁡(i+1)−f⁡(i)|≤1|f(i+1)-f(i)|\leq 1 for m≤i≤nm\leq i\leq n. If f⁡(m)​f​(n)<0f(m)f(n)<0, then f⁡(x)=0f(x)=0 for some integer x∈[m,n]x\in[m,n].

Proposition 3.4.

Let (p,q)∈𝒫(k+1,n)×𝒫(k−1,n)(p,q)\in\mathcal{P}_{(k+1,n)}\times\mathcal{P}_{(k-1,n)} with p=p1​…​pn−1p=p_{1}\dots p_{n-1} and q=q1​…​qn−1q=q_{1}\dots q_{n-1}. There is an index 1≤i≤n−11\leq i\leq n-1 such that p′=p1​…​pi​qi+1​…​qn−1p^{\prime}=p_{1}\dots p_{i}q_{i+1}\dots q_{n-1} and q′=q1​…​qi​pi+1​…​pn−1q^{\prime}=q_{1}\dots q_{i}p_{i+1}\dots p_{n-1} are in 𝒫(k,n)×𝒫(k,n)\mathcal{P}_{(k,n)}\times\mathcal{P}_{(k,n)}.

Proof.

Let N:[0,n−1]→ℤN:[0,n-1]\rightarrow\mathbb{Z} be the function defined by N⁡(0)=−1N(0)=-1 and N⁡(i)=#⁡{r∈[i]|pr=C}−#⁡{r∈[i]|qr=C}−1N(i)=\#\{r\in[i]\ |\ p_{r}=C\}-\#\{r\in[i]\ |\ q_{r}=C\}-1 for 1≤i≤n−11\leq i\leq n-1. Here, |N⁡(i+1)−N⁡(i)|=1|N(i+1)-N(i)|=1 if either pi+1=Cp_{i+1}=C but qi+1≠Cq_{i+1}\neq C, or pi+1≠Cp_{i+1}\neq C but qi+1=Cq_{i+1}=C, and |N⁡(i+1)−N⁡(i)|=0|N(i+1)-N(i)|=0 otherwise. Also, N⁡(0)=−1N(0)=-1 and N⁡(n−1)=1N(n-1)=1 making N⁡(0)​N​(n−1)=−1<0N(0)N(n-1)=-1<0. Therefore, by Theorem 3.3, we have that N⁡(x)=0N(x)=0 for some x∈[n−1]x\in[n-1]. Since N⁡(n−1)−N⁡(x)=1N(n-1)-N(x)=1, we have that there is one more CC step in the remaining subword of pp than there is for qq. Therefore, switching the subwords will have the intended effect. ∎

We are ready to define an injection II from 𝒫(k+1,n)×𝒫(k−1,n)\mathcal{P}_{(k+1,n)}\times\mathcal{P}_{(k-1,n)} to 𝒫(k,n)×𝒫(k,n)\mathcal{P}_{(k,n)}\times\mathcal{P}_{(k,n)}. Given (p,q)∈𝒫(k+1,n)×𝒫(k−1,n)(p,q)\in\mathcal{P}_{(k+1,n)}\times\mathcal{P}_{(k-1,n)} with p=p1​…​pn−1p=p_{1}\dots p_{n-1} and q=q1​…​qn−1q=q_{1}\dots q_{n-1}, choose the largest index ii such that p′=p1​…​pi​qi+1​…​qn−1p^{\prime}=p_{1}\dots p_{i}q_{i+1}\dots q_{n-1} and q′=q1​…​qi​pi+1​…​pn−1q^{\prime}=q_{1}\dots q_{i}p_{i+1}\dots p_{n-1} belongs to 𝒫(k,n)×𝒫(k,n)\mathcal{P}_{(k,n)}\times\mathcal{P}_{(k,n)}. Then I⁡(p,q):=(p′,q′)I(p,q):=(p^{\prime},q^{\prime}). The map is well-defined because of the previous proposition.

Remark.

A step in path q∈𝒫k−1,nq\in\mathcal{P}_{k-1,n} after the index ii is moved exactly 11 step to the right and a step that started at (k1,n1)(k_{1},n_{1}) would now start at (k1+1,n1)(k_{1}+1,n_{1}) in the path q′∈𝒫(k,n)q^{\prime}\in\mathcal{P}_{(k,n)}. Similarly, any step in path p∈𝒫k+1,np\in\mathcal{P}_{k+1,n} would move exactly 11 step to the left after the index ii. Any step that started at (k2,n1)(k_{2},n_{1}) would now start at (k2−1,n1)(k_{2}-1,n_{1}) in the path p′∈𝒫(k,n)p^{\prime}\in\mathcal{P}_{(k,n)}.

3.3 Proofs of Theorems 1.3 and 1.4

Usually, a 22-Motzkin path of length nn is a lattice path starting from (0,0)(0,0) and (n,0)(n,0) that uses an up step U:=(1,1)U:=(1,1), a down step D:=(1,−1)D:=(1,-1), a blue horizontal step H1:=(1,0)H_{1}:=(1,0) and a red horizontal H2:=(1,0)H_{2}:=(1,0). However, we will use the name 22-Motzkin path to mean a lattice path with the steps described above but starting from (0,0)(0,0) and ending in (n,−1)(n,-1) such that the last step is a down step DD and except for the last step, the remaining lattice path lies entirely above the xx-axis.

To obtain a sufficient condition for log-concavity, we will associate a weighted 22-Motzkin path to the pair of paths in 𝒫(k+1,n)×𝒫(k−1,n)\mathcal{P}_{(k+1,n)}\times\mathcal{P}_{(k-1,n)} and use the weighted 22-Motzkin path to create a sufficient condition that ensures the weight of pair of paths increases under the injection defined in the previous subsection. Let (p,q)∈𝒫(k+1,n)×𝒫(k−1,n)(p,q)\in\mathcal{P}_{(k+1,n)}\times\mathcal{P}_{(k-1,n)}. Let ch⁡(p):=pi+1​…​pn−1\ch(p):=p_{i+1}\dots p_{n-1} and ch⁡(q):=qi+1​…​qn−1\ch(q):=q_{i+1}\dots q_{n-1} where ii is largest index such that p1​…​pi​ch⁡(q)p_{1}\dots p_{i}\ch(q) and q1​…​qi​ch⁡(p)q_{1}\dots q_{i}\ch(p) are in 𝒫(k,n)\mathcal{P}_{(k,n)}.

The idea will be that the pair of paths p,qp,q, when looked at from the end, start out with a spacing of 22 ((k−1,n)(k-1,n) and (k+1,n)(k+1,n)), continue with a spacing greater than or equal to 22 and finally, getting down to a spacing of 11 at the index ii prescribed by the injection. We will encode this portion of the paths as a 22-Motzkin path.

To this end, consider the reversal operator rev\rev on words. We start with the two words rev⁡(ch⁡(p))\rev(\ch(p)) and rev⁡(ch⁡(q))\rev(\ch(q)). We build a weighted 22-Motzkin path out of the two words as follows. If the jt​hj^{th} steps of rev⁡(ch⁡(p))\rev(\ch(p)) and rev⁡(ch⁡(q))\rev(\ch(q)) are NN and CC respectively (resp. CC and NN or NN and NN or CC and CC), the jt​hj^{th} step of our weighted 22-Motzkin path is UU (resp. D,H1,H2D,H_{1},H_{2}). The weight of the step in the 22-Motzkin path will be the product of the weight of the corresponding steps in pp and qq.

The fact that such a construction yields a weighted 22-Motzkin path follows the fact that ii is the largest index such that ch⁡(p)\ch(p) has one more CC step than ch⁡(q)\ch(q). The 22-Motzkin path will start at (0,0)(0,0) and end at (n−i,−1)(n-i,-1). Except for the last DD step, the entire path will be above the xx-axis.

The 22-Motzkin path corresponding to our pair of paths is below. The blue steps correspond to H1H_{1} steps.

Let us calculate the weight of the four different steps. The weight of UU step is c⁡(n1,k1)​d​(n1,k2)c(n_{1},k_{1})d(n_{1},k_{2}), and the DD step is d⁡(n1,k1)​c​(n1,k2)d(n_{1},k_{1})c(n_{1},k_{2}). The weight of a H1H_{1} step is c⁡(n1,k1)​c​(n1,k2)c(n_{1},k_{1})c(n_{1},k_{2}). The weight of a H2H_{2} step is d⁡(n1,k1)​d​(n1,k2)d(n_{1},k_{1})d(n_{1},k_{2}).

On a 22-Motzkin path, for each UU step, there is a corresponding DD step. That is if (n2,l2)∈p(n_{2},l_{2})\in p and (n2,l1)∈q(n_{2},l_{1})\in q, there is a (n1,k2)∈p(n_{1},k_{2})\in p and (n1,k1)∈q(n_{1},k_{1})\in q such that the following are true.

  • •

    n2>n1n_{2}>n_{1}, l2>k2>k1l_{2}>k_{2}>k_{1}, l2>l1>k1l_{2}>l_{1}>k_{1},

  • •

    k2−k1=l2−l1+1k_{2}-k_{1}=l_{2}-l_{1}+1,

  • •

    n2−n1≥l2−k2n_{2}-n_{1}\geq l_{2}-k_{2} and n2−n1≥l1−k1n_{2}-n_{1}\geq l_{1}-k_{1}.

We are in a position to prove Theorem 1.3.

Proof of Theorem 1.3.

The weight of a H1H_{1} step is c⁡(n1,k1)​c​(n1,k2)c(n_{1},k_{1})c(n_{1},k_{2}) which goes, under the injection, to a H1H_{1} step whose weight is c⁡(n1,k1+1)​c​(n1,k2−1)c(n_{1},k_{1}+1)c(n_{1},k_{2}-1) (see Remark Remark). Similarly, for H2H_{2}, d⁡(n1,k1)​d​(n1,k2)d(n_{1},k_{1})d(n_{1},k_{2}) goes to d⁡(n1,k1+1)​d​(n1,k2−1)d(n_{1},k_{1}+1)d(n_{1},k_{2}-1). Therefore, Condition (i)(i) ensures that wt⁡(H1)≤wt⁡(I⁡(H1))\wt(H_{1})\leq\wt(I(H_{1})) and wt⁡(H2)≤wt⁡(I⁡(H2))\wt(H_{2})\leq\wt(I(H_{2})).

Similarly, Condition (i​i)(ii) ensures that the product of the weights of a UU and its corresponding DD step in the path is greater after applying the injection.

Finally, Condition (i​i​i)(iii) ensures that the final DD step is greater after applying the injection.

These three conditions ensure that

∑(p,q)∈𝒫(k+1,n)×𝒫(k−1,n)wt⁡(p)​wt⁡(q)≤∑(p′,q′)∈𝒫(k,n)×𝒫(k,n)wt⁡(p′)​wt⁡(q′)\displaystyle\sum_{(p,q)\in\mathcal{P}_{(k+1,n)}\times\mathcal{P}_{(k-1,n)}}\wt(p)\wt(q)\leq\displaystyle\sum_{(p^{\prime},q^{\prime})\in\mathcal{P}_{(k,n)}\times\mathcal{P}_{(k,n)}}\wt(p^{\prime})\wt(q^{\prime})

Therefore, the sequence T⁡(n,k)T(n,k) is log-concave in kk. ∎

Remark.

It should be possible to weaken Condition (i​i​i)(iii) or completely remove it by sufficiently strengthening the other two conditions.

The following is a quick application of this theorem. The Legendre-Stirling numbers were shown to be log-concave [1]. It is easy to verify that the coefficients satisfy the above theorem, therefore, giving us another proof of their log-concavity.

are log-concave in kk for all nn.

For c⁡(n,k),d⁡(n,k)≥0c(n,k),d(n,k)\geq 0, if the triangular array

satisfies the conditions of Theorem 1.3, then for l∈ℕl\in\mathbb{N}, so does the array

Using the two aforementioned results, we can prove the main result of the paper.

Corollary 3.7.

The (l,r)(l,r)-Lah numbers are log-concave in kk for all nn.

Proof.

The (l,r)(l,r)-Lah numbers satisfy the recurrence relation

T⁡(n,k)=(n+k+2​r−3)l​T​(n−1,k)+T⁡(n−1,k−1)T(n,k)=(n+k+2r-3)^{l}\ T(n-1,k)+T(n-1,k-1) (3.2)

with the initial condition T⁡(0,0)=1T(0,0)=1. By Theorem 1.4, we have that this triangular array is log-concave in kk for all nn. ∎

4 Two parameter generalization of Eulerian numbers

Recall that we defined 𝒜r(l)​(n,k)\mathcal{A}_{r}^{(l)}(n,k) to count the number of ll-tuples (f1,…,fl)(f_{1},\dots,f_{l}) such that [r]⊂bl⁡(f1)[r]\subset\bl(f_{1}), |bl⁡(f1)|=k+1|\bl(f_{1})|=k+1, and bl⁡(f1)=⋯=bl⁡(fl)\bl(f_{1})=\dots=\bl(f_{l}). We first start out by proving a recurrence relation for the (l,r)(l,r)-Eulerian numbers. They satisfy a triangular recurrence analogous to the ones satisfied by their Stirling and Lah counterparts.

Proposition 4.1.

For n≥k≥r−1≥0n\geq k\geq r-1\geq 0 and a positive integer ll, we have

𝒜r(l)​(n,k)=(n−k)l​𝒜r(l)​(n−1,k−1)+(k+1)l​𝒜r(l)​(n−1,k)\mathcal{A}_{r}^{(l)}(n,k)=(n-k)^{l}\mathcal{A}_{r}^{(l)}(n-1,k-1)+(k+1)^{l}\mathcal{A}_{r}^{(l)}(n-1,k) (4.1)

and 𝒜r(l)​(r,r)=1\mathcal{A}_{r}^{(l)}(r,r)=1

Proof.

Let ff be a subexceedant function with k+1k+1 elements in bl⁡(f)\bl(f) and [r]⊂bl⁡(f)[r]\subset\bl(f). Then, ff could have been obtained in one of the following two ways.

  1. (i)

    if n∈bl⁡(fi)n\in\bl(f_{i}), its image has one of (n−k)l(n-k)^{l} choices,

  2. (ii)

    if not, then its image has one of (k+1)l(k+1)^{l} choices.

∎

Remark.

By Theorem 1.4, the (l,r)(l,r)-Eulerian numbers are log-concave and therefore, unimodal.

4.1 A bijection

Let π∈𝔖n\pi\in\mathfrak{S}_{n}. Define the block leaders of π\pi, denoted by bl⁡(π)\bl(\pi), as the set of first letters of the increasing runs of π\pi. For example, let π=28​|7|​4​|136|​5\pi=28|7|4|136|5 with bars separating increasing runs. Then, bl⁡(π)={1,2,4,5,7}\bl(\pi)=\{1,2,4,5,7\}. We show that 𝒜r​(n,k):=𝒜r(1)​(n,k)\mathcal{A}_{r}(n,k):=\mathcal{A}^{(1)}_{r}(n,k) also counts the number of permutations π∈𝔖n\pi\in\mathfrak{S}_{n} with kk descents such that [r]⊂bl⁡(π)[r]\subset\bl(\pi).

Starting from a subexceedant function ff that satisfies [r]⊂bl⁡(f)[r]\subset\bl(f) and |bl⁡(f)|=k+1|\bl(f)|=k+1, we give a map Λ\Lambda to a permutation π\pi with kk descents such that [r]⊂bl⁡(π)[r]\subset\bl(\pi) with the additional property that f⁡(bl⁡(f))=bl⁡(π)f(\bl(f))=\bl(\pi).

We give the bijection Λ\Lambda inductively. Start with the empty word and i=1i=1. If f⁡(i)=if(i)=i, add ii to the left of all existing letters. If f⁡(i)∈f⁡([i−1])f(i)\in f([i-1]), then add ii at the end of the increasing run starting at f⁡(i)f(i). If f⁡(i)∉f⁡([i−1])f(i)\notin f([i-1]), then add ii immediately to the left of element f⁡(i)f(i). Increase ii to i+1i+1 and repeat.

Proposition 4.2.

The map Λ\Lambda from the set of subexceedant functions from [n][n] to [n][n] such that [r]∈bl⁡(f)[r]\in\bl(f), |bl⁡(f)|=k+1|\bl(f)|=k+1 to the set of permutations on [n][n] such that [r]∈bl⁡(π)[r]\in\bl(\pi), |bl⁡(π)|=k+1|\bl(\pi)|=k+1 is a bijection such that f⁡(bl⁡(f))=bl⁡(Λ⁡(f))f(\bl(f))=\bl(\Lambda(f)).

Proof.

It is clear that the function Λ\Lambda is a bijection as we are able to describe its inverse. It remains to show that f⁡(bl⁡(f))=bl⁡(Λ⁡(f))f(\bl(f))=\bl(\Lambda(f)). Suppose f⁡(i)∉f⁡([i−1])f(i)\notin f([i-1]), then ii goes behind f⁡(i)f(i), making f⁡(i)f(i) the first element of an increasing run. Similarly, the elements ii such that f⁡(i)=if(i)=i are added to the leftmost position and therefore, are first elements of an increasing run. Therefore, the block leaders of Λ⁡(f)\Lambda(f) are exactly the elements of f⁡(bl⁡(f))f(\bl(f)). ∎

We have the following connection between the rr-Stirling number of the second kind and 𝒜r​(n,k)\mathcal{A}_{r}(n,k). When r=1r=1, this identity specialises to Bóna [4, Theorem 1.18].

Theorem 4.3.

For n≥k≥r−1≥0n\geq k\geq r-1\geq 0, we have

k!​Sr​(n,k)=∑i=rk𝒜r​(n,i−1)​(n−ik−i).k!S_{r}(n,k)=\sum_{i=r}^{k}\mathcal{A}_{r}(n,i-1)\binom{n-i}{k-i}. (4.2)
Proof.

The LHS is the number of ordered partitions Π\Pi of [n][n] into kk blocks such that [r]⊂bl⁡(Π)[r]\subset\bl(\Pi). We need to show that RHS counts the same objects. Let π∈𝔖n\pi\in\mathfrak{S}_{n} with i−1i-1 descents and [r]⊂bl⁡(π)[r]\subset\bl(\pi). The ii increasing runs of π\pi give us an ordered partition of [n][n]. Now, the number of blocks is ii, which can be smaller than kk. However, we can make more blocks by making splits of the increasing runs. We need to make k−ik-i splits. This can be done by choosing k−ik-i of the n−in-i different places where we can split.

We just need to now show that the ordered partitions thus formed are all distinct. However, given an ordered partition Π\Pi of [n][n], we can arrange the blocks in ascending order internally and read from left to right a unique permutation and the choice of splitting from which it can be obtained. ∎

Corollary 4.4.

For n≥k≥r−1≥0n\geq k\geq r-1\geq 0, we have

𝒜r​(n,k−1)=∑i=1k(−1)k−i​Sr​(n,i)​(n−ik−i)​i!\mathcal{A}_{r}(n,k-1)=\sum_{i=1}^{k}(-1)^{k-i}S_{r}(n,i)\binom{n-i}{k-i}i! (4.3)
Proof.

Equation 4.2 can be rewritten as ∑k=rn𝒜r​(n,k−1)​(t+1)k=∑k=rnk!​Sr​(n,k)​tn−k\sum_{k=r}^{n}\mathcal{A}_{r}(n,k-1)(t+1)^{k}=\sum_{k=r}^{n}k!S_{r}(n,k)t^{n-k}. The corollary follows from the substitution t→t−1t\rightarrow t-1. ∎

4.2 Palindromicity of the associated generalised Eulerian polynomials

In this section, let us restrict our attention to the case when r=1r=1. We define associated (l,1)(l,1)-Eulerian polynomials to be

𝒜n(l)​(t):=∑k=0n−1𝒜(l)​(n,k)​tk.\mathcal{A}_{n}^{(l)}(t):=\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}\mathcal{A}^{(l)}(n,k)t^{k}. (4.4)

It is not immediately clear that this polynomial is palindromic. To that end, we define

𝒜n(l)​(s,t):=∑k=0n−1𝒜(l)​(n,k)​sk​tn−1−k.\mathcal{A}_{n}^{(l)}(s,t):=\displaystyle\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}\mathcal{A}^{(l)}(n,k)s^{k}t^{n-1-k}. (4.5)

We show that the polynomial 𝒜n(l)​(s,t)\mathcal{A}_{n}^{(l)}(s,t) is symmetric in s,ts,t, i.e., 𝒜n(l)​(s,t)=𝒜n(l)​(s,t)\mathcal{A}_{n}^{(l)}(s,t)=\mathcal{A}_{n}^{(l)}(s,t). Let 𝒟s=s​∂∂s\mathcal{D}_{s}=s\frac{\partial}{\partial s} and 𝒟t=t​∂∂t\mathcal{D}_{t}=t\frac{\partial}{\partial t} in ℚ⁡[s,t]\mathbb{Q}[s,t]. The symmetry becomes apparent from the following proposition.

Proposition 4.5.

The polynomials 𝒜n(l)​(s,t)\mathcal{A}^{(l)}_{n}(s,t) satisfy the following partial differential equation.

𝒜n(l)​(s,t)=1s​𝒟sl​(s​t​𝒜n−1(l)​(s,t))+1t​𝒟tl​(s​t​𝒜n−1(l)​(s,t))\mathcal{A}^{(l)}_{n}(s,t)=\frac{1}{s}\mathcal{D}_{s}^{l}(st\mathcal{A}^{(l)}_{n-1}(s,t))+\frac{1}{t}\mathcal{D}_{t}^{l}(st\mathcal{A}^{(l)}_{n-1}(s,t)) (4.6)

with 𝒜0(l)​(s,t)=1\mathcal{A}^{(l)}_{0}(s,t)=1 initially.

Proof.
𝒟sl​(s​t​𝒜n(l)​(s,t))\displaystyle\mathcal{D}_{s}^{l}(st\mathcal{A}^{(l)}_{n}(s,t)) =\displaystyle= t​𝒟sl​(s​𝒜n(l)​(s,t))\displaystyle t\mathcal{D}_{s}^{l}(s\mathcal{A}^{(l)}_{n}(s,t))
=\displaystyle= t⁡(𝒟sl​(∑k=0n𝒜(l)​(n,k)​sk+1​tn−1−k))\displaystyle t\bigg(\mathcal{D}_{s}^{l}(\sum_{k=0}^{n}\mathcal{A}^{(l)}(n,k)s^{k+1}t^{n-1-k})\bigg)
=\displaystyle= ∑k=0n−1(k+1)l​𝒜(l)​(n,k)​sk+1​tn−k\displaystyle\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}(k+1)^{l}\mathcal{A}^{(l)}(n,k)s^{k+1}t^{n-k}

Similarly,

𝒟tl​(s​t​𝒜n(l)​(s,t))\displaystyle\mathcal{D}_{t}^{l}(st\mathcal{A}^{(l)}_{n}(s,t)) =\displaystyle= s​𝒟tl​(t​𝒜n(l)​(s,t))\displaystyle s\mathcal{D}_{t}^{l}(t\mathcal{A}^{(l)}_{n}(s,t))
=\displaystyle= s⁡(𝒟tl​(∑k=0n𝒜(l)​(n,k)​sk​tn−k))\displaystyle s\bigg(\mathcal{D}_{t}^{l}(\sum_{k=0}^{n}\mathcal{A}^{(l)}(n,k)s^{k}t^{n-k})\bigg)
=\displaystyle= ∑k=0n−1(n−k)l​𝒜(l)​(n,k)​sk+1​tn−k\displaystyle\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}(n-k)^{l}\mathcal{A}^{(l)}(n,k)s^{k+1}t^{n-k}

Therefore, the RHS of the proposition evaluates the polynomial

∑k=0n−1(k+1)l​𝒜(l)​(n,k)​sk​tn−k+∑k=0n−1(n−k)l​𝒜(l)​(n,k)​sk+1​tn−1−k\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}(k+1)^{l}\mathcal{A}^{(l)}(n,k)s^{k}t^{n-k}+\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}(n-k)^{l}\mathcal{A}^{(l)}(n,k)s^{k+1}t^{n-1-k}

Comparing coefficients with (4.5) gives us the result. ∎

A palindromic polynomial p⁡(x)=∑k=0nan​xkp(x)=\displaystyle\sum_{k=0}^{n}a_{n}x^{k} is said to be gamma-positive of center of symmetry ⌊n2⌋\lfloor\frac{n}{2}\rfloor if it can be written in the form p⁡(x)=∑i=0⌊n2⌋γn,i​ti​(1+t)n−2​ip(x)=\displaystyle\sum_{i=0}^{\lfloor\frac{n}{2}\rfloor}\gamma_{n,i}t^{i}(1+t)^{n-2i}. In light of the palindromicity of these polynomials, it would be the next natural question to ask if they are gamma-positive. It is not difficult to show that these polynomials are gamma-positive when l=2l=2. The following is the recurrence 4.5 for the polynomials written out.

Proposition 4.6.

The polynomials 𝒜n(2)​(s,t)\mathcal{A}_{n}^{(2)}(s,t) satisfy the recurrence relation

𝒜n(2)​(s,t)=(s+t)​𝒜n−1(2)​(s,t)+3​s​t​(∂∂s+∂∂t)​𝒜n−1(2)​(s,t)+s​t​(s​∂2∂s2+t​∂2∂t2)​𝒜n−1(2)​(s,t)\mathcal{A}_{n}^{(2)}(s,t)=(s+t)\mathcal{A}_{n-1}^{(2)}(s,t)+3st(\frac{\partial}{\partial s}+\frac{\partial}{\partial t})\mathcal{A}_{n-1}^{(2)}(s,t)+st(s\frac{\partial^{2}}{\partial s^{2}}+t\frac{\partial^{2}}{\partial t^{2}})\mathcal{A}_{n-1}^{(2)}(s,t) (4.7)

with 𝒜0(2)​(s,t)=1\mathcal{A}_{0}^{(2)}(s,t)=1 initially.

It is straightforward to show that

s​∂2∂s2+t​∂2∂t2s\frac{\partial^{2}}{\partial s^{2}}+t\frac{\partial^{2}}{\partial t^{2}}

sends an element of the gamma-basis (s​t)i​(s+t)n−1−i(st)^{i}(s+t)^{n-1-i} to a positive linear combination of gamma basis elements as do the other two terms. Since these are linear operators, we have that the polynomials are gamma-positive by induction. If we set s=1s=1, we get

Proposition 4.7.

The polynomials 𝒜n2​(t):=∑k=0n−1𝒜(2)​(n,k)​tk\mathcal{A}_{n}^{2}(t):=\displaystyle\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}\mathcal{A}^{(2)}(n,k)t^{k} are gamma-positive for all n≥2n\geq 2.

Here are the polynomials 𝒜n3​(t)\mathcal{A}_{n}^{3}(t) and their expansion in the gamma-basis.

𝒜33​(t)\displaystyle\mathcal{A}_{3}^{3}(t) =\displaystyle= 1+16​t+t2=(1+t)2+14​t\displaystyle 1+16t+t^{2}=(1+t)^{2}+14t
𝒜43​(t)\displaystyle\mathcal{A}_{4}^{3}(t) =\displaystyle= 1+155​t+155​t2+t3=(1+t)3+152​t​(1+t)\displaystyle 1+155t+155t^{2}+t^{3}=(1+t)^{3}+152t(1+t)
𝒜53​(t)\displaystyle\mathcal{A}_{5}^{3}(t) =\displaystyle= 1+1304​t+8370​t2+1304​t3+t4=(1+t)4+1300​t​(1+t)2+5764​t2\displaystyle 1+1304t+8370t^{2}+1304t^{3}+t^{4}=(1+t)^{4}+1300t(1+t)^{2}+5764t^{2}
𝒜63​(t)\displaystyle\mathcal{A}_{6}^{3}(t) =\displaystyle= 1+10557​t+309446​t2+309446​t3+10557​t4+t5=(1+t)5+10552​t​(1+t)3+277780​t2​(1+t)\displaystyle 1+10557t+309446t^{2}+309446t^{3}+10557t^{4}+t^{5}=(1+t)^{5}+10552t(1+t)^{3}+277780t^{2}(1+t)
Remark.

We know that the Eulerian polynomials are gamma-positive and we have proved that the (2,1)(2,1)-Eulerian polynomials are gamma-positive. Based on the limited data that we were able to compute, the (l,1)(l,1)-Eulerian polynomials seem to be gamma-positive for all l≥3l\geq 3.

Remark.

A similar remark can be made about real-rootedness. The Eulerian polynomials are known to be real rooted due to Frobenius [7]. From our limited data, it appears that the (l,1)(l,1)-Eulerian polynomials are real rooted for l≥2l\geq 2.
